items.title: Yemen Market and Trade Bulletin October 2026 - Issued on 21st November 2026
items.author: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations
items.content:
Country: Yemen
Source: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations

Please refer to the attached file.

SHORT-TERM OUTLOOK AND IMPLICATIONS ON FOOD SECURITY:

While Yemen’s acute food security crisis—with roughly 18.7 million people (over half the population) facing acute food insecurity (IPC Phase 3 or worse)—remains driven by heavy import dependency, rising food and fuel prices, severe humanitarian funding deficits, and climate and rainfall shocks, conditions have deteriorated sharply amid renewed frontline conflict and regional spillover effects. Since July 2026—and intensifying in September around Ta’iz, along the western coast, and across southern flashpoints—escalating hostilities and displacement have placed severe strain on overstretched services and existing displaced populations, while access constraints and road/maritime disruptions have slowed trade flows, pushed up freight and fuel costs, and restricted humanitarian reach. These compounding shocks—aggravated by funding shortfalls and climate stress—are eroding household purchasing power and driving acute deprivation, with millions facing IPC Phase 3 or worse conditions and localized emergency/catastrophe risks in late 2026.

KEY HIGHLIGHTS:

  • EXCHANGE RATES: Currency stability continued. The exchange rate remained broadly stable in GoY-controlled areas, trading 4% below its level a year earlier and 8% below the three-year average—indicating a firmer Yemeni rial against both benchmarks.
  • FOOD PRICES: Key staples became more expensive. In GoY-controlled areas, flour and basmati rice prices rose by 7.4% and 6.3% month-on-month, while sunflower oil and beans increased by 3.3% and 3.6%, respectively.
  • MINIMUM FOOD BASKET (MFB): Food-basket costs increased. Minimum Food Basket (MFB) costs in GoY-controlled areas rose 2% month-on-month from August, standing 7% above September 2025 levels and 2% above the three-year average—further squeezing household food affordability.
  • FOOD AND FUEL IMPORTS: Grain arrivals in GoY areas declined sharply. Recorded wheat and flour imports fell by 1.5% nationally and by 42.5% through southern ports. Recorded petrol and diesel imports also decreased by 9.9%; however, the absence of northern records limits the interpretation of this trend.
  • FUEL PRICES: Official diesel eased but remained elevated. Diesel prices fell by 4.5% month-on-month while petrol remained broadly stable; however, both fuels stayed substantially above last year's levels and their three-year averages.
  • TERMS OF TRADE (ToT): Flour purchasing power weakened. The Government of Yemen’s casual labor-to-flour terms of trade declined by 7.2% month-on-month and 23.1% year-on-year. Agricultural and composite livestock-to-flour ratios also decreased.
  • CASUAL LABOR WAGE RATES: Daily rates barely adjusted. In GoY-controlled areas, casual wages slipped 0.4% month-on-month and remained 9.7% below year-ago levels, while agricultural wages edged up by 0.4%.
  • LIVESTOCK PRICES: Modest recovery offered limited relief. Goat and local sheep prices increased month-on-month by 1.6% and 2.4%, respectively, but remained below their levels from the previous year.

items.creator: Education Cluster
items.title: DR Congo: Evaluation conjointe des besoins en matière d’Education et Protection RDC-2026
items.author: Education Cluster
items.content:
Country: Democratic Republic of the Congo
Sources: Education Cluster, Save the Children, UN Children's Fund

Please refer to the attached file.

Le rapport de l’évaluation conjointe des besoins d’Education et de Protection menée en collaboration avec le secteur de la Protection met en évidence les résultats suivants :

  • Taux d’abandon de 12,5 % au cours de l’année scolaire 2025-2026, principalement lié aux difficultés socio-économiques des ménages, aux déplacements forcés, aux travaux domestiques, ainsi qu’aux mariages et grossesses précoces.
  • 131 établissements sur 266 (50 %) rapportent des absences scolaires liées à la gestion des menstruations.
  • 76 responsables d’établissements sur 266 (28%) affirment que les établissements ont subi des pillages ou vols perpétrés par des groupes armés depuis le début de l’année 2026, tandis que 47 sur 266 (18%) ont relevé l’occupation de salles de classe par des forces ou groupes armés.
  • L’inclusion des enfants en situation de handicap demeure limitée, avec peu de mesures spécifiques favorisant leur participation et leur maintien à l’école.
  • Seuls 51 établissements sur 266 (19 %) disposent d’un accès à l’eau potable provenant de leur principale source d’approvisionnement.
  • 114 établissements (43 %) ne disposent pas de latrines séparées pour les filles et les garçons.
  • 101 établissements sur 266 (38 %) signalent la présence d’enfants présentant des signes de détresse psychosociale, notamment des cauchemars, une tristesse persistante, une anxiété élevée, de la fatigue extrême, des comportements violents ou de l’isolement.
  • Seuls 70 établissements sur 266 (26%) disposent d’un mécanisme de référencement VBG adapté aux enfants et permettant l’orientation vers des services spécialisés.

Malgré ces défis, les consultations avec les enfants montrent que l’école reste perçue comme un espace de protection, de stabilité et d’espoir. Comme l’a souligné un enfant de 8 à 11 ans : « A l’école, on étudie et on oublie la guerre. »

items.title: Lebanon: Inter-Agency Response Update - (15 November 2026)
items.author: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs
items.content:
Country: Lebanon
Source: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs

Please refer to the attached file.

HIGHLIGHTS

  • Limited alternatives for IDPs amid ongoing consolidation of collective shelters. Some 1200 IDPs moved out of collective shelters during the first two weeks of the month, underscoring limited alternatives available for those unable to return home. Planned shelter closures continue, requiring coordinated efforts to identify suitable relocation options and ensure that IDPs can relocate safely and voluntarily.
  • Food insecurity remains widespread, with further deterioration projected in 2027. According to the latest IPC analysis, 1.05 million people face crisis or worse levels of acute food insecurity currently, projected to rise to 1.15 million from March 2027.
  • Increasing winterization needs. Colder weather and rising seasonal expenses exacerbate vulnerability among conflict-affected households, particularly IDPs and returnees living in inadequate shelters.

items.creator: World Food Programme
items.title: oPt: WFP Palestine External Situation Report, 21 November (Reporting Period: 1- 31 October 2026)
items.author: World Food Programme
items.content:
Country: occupied Palestinian territory
Source: World Food Programme

Please refer to the attached file.

HIGHLIGHTS

  • More than three years into the crisis in Gaza, and one year into the ceasefire, displaced families are facing a fourth winter in
    tents. Although humanitarian assistance and commercial supplies increased following the October 2025 ceasefire, they remain
    insufficient against the scale of needs, and the crisis is far from over.
  • Some 1.4 million people, or two-thirds of the population, are acutely food insecure, with deteriorating weather conditions
    expected to further deplete their already limited capacity to safely store food and access cooking fuel.
  • Funding shortfalls have already forced WFP to cut monthly food assistance by one-third in Gaza and by half in the West Bank,
    heightening the risk of further deterioration in food security as winter compounds existing vulnerabilities.

items.creator: Education Cluster
items.title: oPt: Gaza Strip | Learning Spaces Assessment Report (November 2026)
items.author: Education Cluster
items.content:
Country: occupied Palestinian territory
Source: Education Cluster

Please refer to the attached file.

The assessment covered 962 learning spaces across Gaza’s five governorates between 21 May and 12 August 2026, reporting 581,111 enrolments and 15,709 teachers. In the absence of permanent education infrastructure, Temporary learning spaces, community-led initiatives and private learning spaces have sustained education despite severe disruption. Most learning spaces reported being fully functional and using learning content consistent with that of the Ministry of Education and Higher Education (MoEHE). These responses provide limited information about instructional time, safety, inclusion or the resources available to learners.

The assessment identified substantial pressure on the learning spaces. A ten-point checklist classified 362 as good, 494 as at risk and 106 as critical. At-risk spaces remain operational but need improvements to support children’s safety, wellbeing and learning. Critical spaces are partly operating, temporarily closed or missing several basic facilities and services. These categories guide support priorities; they do not assess building safety. Limited covered space and widespread double or triple shifts constrain provision. Multiple shifts expand access but may reduce teaching time and increase pressure on facilities. Nearly half of assessed spaces reported additional demand from displaced children or waiting lists.

Protection, water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH), and basic services remain uneven. Children face barriers linked to insecurity, distance, transport, psychological distress and household responsibilities. Protection referral mechanisms and disaster preparedness measures are not consistently available, particularly in community-led initiatives. Gaps in safe drinking water, appropriate sanitation, electricity and first-aid capacity affect children’s safety, dignity and participation.

Disability inclusion requires attention. Although children with disabilities were enrolled across many spaces, accessible facilities, inclusive sanitation and adapted learning materials were less widely available. Enrolment alone does not demonstrate meaningful participation. Accessibility, adapted materials, assistive products, transport and specialist referrals need to be integrated into programme planning and budgets.

Most learning spaces reported using clearly defined learning content. Shortages of furniture and educational materials constrained teaching. Training and psychosocial support for teachers were uneven, particularly in community-led initiatives, where reliance on volunteers also raises concerns about staff retention and continuity. Community participation provides a foundation for local accountability, although women’s and learners’ representation needs strengthening.

The assessment provides a common evidence base for the Cluster’s 2027 planning, advocacy and resource mobilisation to sustain access, improve learning conditions and support pathways to recognised formal education. Its central finding is that sustaining enrolment requires conditions that enable children to attend regularly, participate meaningfully and learn. The findings describe assessed learning spaces and will be considered alongside other evidence on learning outcomes and children’s wider education needs across Gaza. Section 1.1 sets out the priorities for collective action.

What does this mean for the response

  • Agree joint priorities and responsibilities: Coordinate partners to address urgent needs in the 106 critical learning spaces and develop improvement plans for the 494 at-risk spaces, with clear responsibilities and follow-up on gaps.
  • Mobilise resources for complete learning packages: Promote shared minimum requirements and coordinated funding for safe, weather-resistant spaces, supported teachers, inclusive water and sanitation, learning materials, learning recovery and protection services.
  • Coordinate expansion in high-demand areas: Work with MoEHE, local authorities and partners to verify unmet demand, identify suitable locations and align partner coverage as enrolment grows, particularly in Khan Younis.
  • Strengthen inclusion and support community-led provision: Integrate accessibility and disability inclusion into joint planning, budgets and referral arrangements. Connect community-led initiatives with training, supervision, personnel support and protection services while preserving local ownership.
  • Harmonise information and accountability: Maintain a shared learning-space register and common reporting definitions with MoEHE and partners. Use regular monitoring and community feedback to identify gaps, avoid duplication and track attendance, safety, participation and learning.

items.title: Ecuador: Latin America & The Caribbean Weekly Situation Update as of 20 November 2026
items.author: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs
items.content:
Countries: Ecuador, Bolivia (Plurinational State of), El Salvador, Guatemala, Haiti, Honduras, Mexico, Panama, Peru, United States of America
Source: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs

Please refer to the attached Infographic.

KEY FIGURES

  • 7.9K people displaced in Haiti since mid-October
  • 3.2M people could face crisis-level food insecurity in Guatemala
  • 62K people affected by El Niño-related rains in Ecuador

HAITI: VIOLENCE & DISPLACEMENT

Escalating armed violence across the country is deepening humanitarian needs and restricting access, particularly in densely populated areas of the capital, Port-au-Prince. Since mid-October, violence in Croix-des-Bouquets, on the capital’s outskirts, has displaced about 2,000 people. Nearly 90 per cent are staying with host families and the rest in five informal sites. In late October, attacks in Arcahaie and Cabaret, north-west of the capital, displaced more than 5,900 people. Each new wave puts more strain on stretched host communities. Violence killed an estimated 4,200 people nationwide between January and September, and some 1.5 million people remain displaced. The UN continues to call for the protection of civilians and for safe access to health facilities, schools and other essential services.

CENTRAL AMERICA: FOOD SECURITY

El Niño-related drought is deepening hunger in Central America’s Dry Corridor, where families are running out of food after a failed harvest. An Oxfam assessment of 354 communities in Guatemala, Honduras and El Salvador found that nearly 8 in 10 maize-producing households lost 75 to 100 per cent of their crop this year. Most now have food reserves for three weeks or less. The drought is also cutting rural incomes: the region’s sugar harvest, a key source of seasonal work, could fall by up to 21 per cent. Projections show about 3.2 million people in Guatemala and 1.8 million in Honduras facing Crisis (IPC Phase 3) or worse levels of food insecurity, while up to 249,000 people in El Salvador could face food insecurity.

SOUTH AMERICA: EL NIÑO

El Niño-related rains are worsening along South America’s Pacific coast. In Ecuador, the number of people affected is 62,000 as of 18 November, up from about 65,000 a week earlier, according to the National Secretariat for Risk Management (SNGR). Of these, 36,729 have lost their homes or livelihoods. The rains have led to 16 deaths, damaged more than 25,600 homes, affected over 2,280 schools and 13,000 hectares of crops, and reached all 24 provinces. The National Institute of Meteorology and Hydrology (INAMHI) forecasts heavier rain through 21 November. In northern Peru, overflowing streams have cut off several communities in Tumbes, and forecasters warn the Piura River could rise. On 19 November, authorities placed nine Piura and Tumbes provinces under red alert.

REGIONAL: HEALTH ALERTS

Measles and malaria are spreading across the region as gaps in immunization and disease control persist. As of 13 November, PAHO had confirmed 58,213 measles cases and 82 deaths in the Americas this year, more than four times the number for the same period in 2025. Guatemala accounts for most of them, with more than 34,700 cases and 53 deaths. Bolivia, Mexico and the United States have now lost their measles elimination status. Panama has recorded more than 6,700 malaria cases, mainly in the East Panama, Guna Yala and Darién health regions. They include an outbreak of 161 cases in Ancón, an area of the capital, Panama City, where malaria is not endemic. On 16 November, the Ministry of Health declared a national health alert.

items.title: Ecuador: Latinoamérica y El Caribe Resumen de Situación Semanal al 20 de noviembre 2026
items.author: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs
items.content:
Countries: Ecuador, Bolivia (Plurinational State of), El Salvador, Guatemala, Haiti, Honduras, Mexico, Panama, Peru, United States of America
Source: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs

Please refer to the attached Infographic.

CIFRAS CLAVE

  • 7,9K personas desplazadas en Haití desde mediados de octubre
  • 3,2M personas podrían enfrentar inseguridad alimentaria de nivel Crisis en Guatemala
  • 62K personas afectadas por lluvias asociadas a El Niño en Ecuador

HAITÍ: VIOLENCIA Y DESPLAZAMIENTO

La escalada de violencia armada agrava las necesidades y limita el acceso humanitario, sobre todo en zonas densamente pobladas de la capital, Puerto Príncipe. Desde mediados de octubre, la violencia en Croix-des-Bouquets, en las afueras de la capital, ha desplazado a unas 2.000 personas. Casi el 90% se aloja con familias de acogida y el resto, en cinco sitios informales. A finales de octubre, ataques en Arcahaie y Cabaret, al noroeste de la capital, desplazaron a más de 5.900 personas. Cada nueva ola presiona aún más a comunidades de acogida ya desbordadas. La violencia dejó unas 4.200 víctimas mortales entre enero y septiembre, y 1,5 millones de personas siguen desplazadas en el país. La ONU sigue pidiendo proteger a la población civil y garantizar el acceso seguro a centros de salud, escuelas y otros servicios esenciales.

CENTROAMÉRICA: SEGURIDAD ALIMENTARIA

La sequía asociada a El Niño agrava el hambre en el Corredor Seco centroamericano, donde las familias se quedan sin alimentos tras una mala cosecha. Una evaluación de Oxfam en 354 comunidades de Guatemala, Honduras y El Salvador reveló que casi 8 de cada 10 hogares productores de maíz perdieron del 75% al 100% de su cosecha este año. La mayoría tiene reservas de alimentos para tres semanas o menos. La sequía también reduce los ingresos rurales: la cosecha de caña de azúcar de la región, una fuente clave de empleo temporal, podría caer hasta un 21%. Según las proyecciones, unos 3,2 millones de personas en Guatemala y 1,8 millones en Honduras enfrentarán inseguridad alimentaria en Crisis (Fase 3 de la CIF) o peor, y hasta 249.000 en El Salvador podrían padecerla.

SURAMÉRICA: EL NIÑO

Las lluvias asociadas a El Niño cobran fuerza en la costa pacífica de Sudamérica. En Ecuador, las personas afectadas sumaban 62.000 al 18 de noviembre, frente a unas 65.000 una semana antes, según la Secretaría Nacional de Gestión de Riesgos (SNGR). De ellas, 36.729 perdieron su vivienda o medios de vida. Las lluvias causaron 16 víctimas mortales, dañaron más de 25.600 viviendas, afectaron más de 2.280 escuelas y 13.000 hectáreas de cultivos, y llegaron a las 24 provincias. El Instituto Nacional de Meteorología e Hidrología (INAMHI) prevé lluvias más intensas hasta el 21 de noviembre. En el norte de Perú, el desborde de arroyos aisló a varias comunidades en Tumbes, y los meteorólogos advierten que el río Piura podría crecer. El 19 de noviembre, las autoridades declararon la alerta roja en nueve provincias de Piura y Tumbes

REGIONAL: ALERTAS SANITARIAS

El sarampión y la malaria se propagan en la región ante brechas persistentes en inmunización y control de enfermedades. Al 13 de noviembre, la OPS había confirmado 58.213 casos de sarampión y 82 defunciones en las Américas este año, más del cuádruple que en el mismo periodo de 2025. Guatemala concentra la mayoría, con más de 34.700 casos y 53 defunciones. Bolivia, México y Estados Unidos ya perdieron su estatus de eliminación del sarampión. Panamá registra más de 6.700 casos de malaria, sobre todo en las regiones de salud de Panamá Este, Guna Yala y Darién. Incluyen un brote de 161 casos en Ancón, zona de la capital, Ciudad de Panamá, donde la malaria no es endémica. El 16 de noviembre, el Ministerio de Salud declaró una alerta sanitaria nacional.

Countries: Ecuador, Bolivia (Plurinational State of), El Salvador, Guatemala, Haiti, Honduras, Mexico, Panama, Peru, United States of America
Source: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs

Please refer to the attached Infographic.
CIFRAS CLAVE
7,9K personas desplazadas en Haití desde mediados de octubre
3,2M personas podrían enfrentar inseguridad alimentaria de nivel Crisis en Guatemala
62K personas afectadas por lluvias asociadas a El Niño en Ecuador
HAITÍ: VIOLENCIA Y DESPLAZAMIENTO
La escalada de violencia armada agrava las necesidades y limita el acceso humanitario, sobre todo en zonas densamente pobladas de la capital, Puerto Príncipe. Desde mediados de octubre, la violencia en Croix-des-Bouquets, en las afueras de la capital, ha desplazado a unas 2.000 personas. Casi el 90% se aloja con familias de acogida y el resto, en cinco sitios informales. A finales de octubre, ataques en Arcahaie y Cabaret, al noroeste de la capital, desplazaron a más de 5.900 personas. Cada nueva ola presiona aún más a comunidades de acogida ya desbordadas. La violencia dejó unas 4.200 víctimas mortales entre enero y septiembre, y 1,5 millones de personas siguen desplazadas en el país. La ONU sigue pidiendo proteger a la población civil y garantizar el acceso seguro a centros de salud, escuelas y otros servicios esenciales.

IOM’s Situation Report No. 20 covers the Hurricane Melissa response in Jamaica from November 2025 to October 2026. While emergency debris-removal, cash-for-work, non-food-item and psychosocial support activities have concluded, shelter recovery continues: 4,105 households have received repair assistance, and four community centres have been repaired to support emergency shelter capacity. The report highlights progress, remaining priorities and the partnerships needed to sustain recovery and strengthen resilience.

items.title: Haiti: Haïti : Cluster Abris, Terre et Coordination des Sites (SLSC) – Aperçu mensuel, octobre 2026
items.author: CCCM Cluster
items.content:
Country: Haiti
Sources: CCCM Cluster, Housing, Land, and Property Area of Responsibility, Shelter Cluster, Shelter, Land and Site Coordination Cluster

Please refer to the attached file.

Cet aperçu mensuel présente la réponse du Cluster Abris, Terre et Coordination des Sites (SLSC) en Haïti : abris et biens non alimentaires (BNA), coordination et gestion des sites (CCCM), et logement, terre et biens (LTB). C'est le premier numéro commun depuis la fusion des clusters Abris/BNA et CCCM.

Faits saillants d'octobre 2026 :

  • Contexte : 1,5 million de personnes déplacées internes (DTM, Round 14), dont 223 821 vivent dans 221 sites actifs.
  • Nouveaux déplacements : quatre alertes ETT suivies en octobre concernent près de 29 000 personnes en Artibonite et dans l'Ouest. Fin octobre, les inondations ont fait 59 420 sinistrés dans l'Ouest et le Grand Sud.
  • Abris et BNA : 54 144 personnes assistées en octobre par 8 partenaires dans 15 communes. Depuis janvier, 345 902 personnes ont été assistées par 20 partenaires dans 44 communes, soit 59 % de la cible du HNRP 2026.
  • Gestion des sites : 128 sites sur 221 (58 %) ont un gestionnaire et abritent 84 % des PDI en site. 93 sites, où vivent 35 756 personnes, restent sans gestionnaire, dont 45 en Artibonite.
  • Redevabilité : 299 plaintes et retours reçus en octobre (4 327 depuis janvier) et 1 039 visites dans les centres de ressources communautaires.
  • Lacunes : aucune activité Abris/BNA rapportée en 2026 dans les Nippes, le Nord et le Nord-Est. L'insécurité limite l'accès à Petite-Rivière de l'Artibonite, Verrettes et Arcahaie.
  • Financement : 27,0 M$ reçus sur 77,6 M$ requis (35 %). 50,5 M$ restent à mobiliser.

items.title: Central African Republic: Situation Report No. 94, as of 17 November 2026
items.author: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs
items.content:
Country: Central African Republic
Source: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs

Please refer to the attached file.

HIGHLIGHTS

  • Despite a still volatile context, some humanitarian movements have resumed around Zémio.
  • Infrastructure has been installed in Ouham-Pendé to help prevent agro-pastoral conflicts and reduce tensions between herders and farmers.
  • 3,900 students received school kits in Kaga-Bandoro and M’brès.

GENERAL CONTEXT

Haut-Mbomou Prefecture – South-East

The security situation remains volatile in the Zémio area, despite a relative improvement recently observed along certain roads around the town. In this context, humanitarian actors have gradually resumed some movements and activities in areas affected by movement restrictions that have been in place since September. A limited resumption of civilian movement has also been observed on the main road corridors, while staff from peripheral health facilities have been able to travel to Zémio to replenish medical supplies. No incidents have recently been reported on these routes. A humanitarian organization also conducted movements along the Zémio-Dembia axis to carry out assessments. Given the continuing volatility of the security environment, humanitarian partners are closely monitoring developments and maintaining existing security and risk-management measures.

HUMANITARIAN NEEDS AND RESPONSE

Health

Haute-Kotto Prefecture – Central

On 11 November, the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) and its partner International Medical Corps (IMC) concluded their campaign providing comprehensive care for women living with obstetric fistula. A total of 33 patients received specialized treatment in Bria, with an 88 per cent success rate. 15 other patients faced transportation challenges in reaching Bria from Ndele in Bamingui-Bangoran Prefecture. To improve access to services in that area, a second two-week campaign is being conducted in Ndele from 12 to 26 November 2026.

Multi-sector

Vakaga Prefecture – North-East

On 11 November, the NGO COHEB, under a labour-intensive work project implemented through the Emergency Project to Support the Stabilization and Recovery of Refugees and Host Communities in the Lake Chad Basin (PASRRC), distributed cash assistance to 400 beneficiaries, including 150 Sudanese refugees and 250 members of host communities. Through the cash-for-work approach, each beneficiary received 30,000 CFA francs to support livelihoods and meet priority household needs.

items.title: CAR: République centrafricaine : Rapport de situation N° 94 au 17 novembre 2026
items.author: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs
items.content:
Country: Central African Republic
Source: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs

Please refer to the attached file.

FAITS SAILLANTS

  • Malgré un contexte toujours volatil, certains mouvements humanitaires ont repris autour de Zémio.
  • Des infrastructures pour prévenir les conflits agro-pastoraux et réduire les tensions entre éleveurs et agriculteurs dans l’Ouham-Pendé.
  • 3 900 élèves reçoivent des kits scolaires à Kaga-Bandoro et M’brès.

CONTEXTE GÉNÉRAL

Préfecture du Haut-Mbomou – Sud-Est

La situation sécuritaire demeure volatile dans la région de Zémio, malgré une accalmie relative observée récemment sur certains axes routiers autour de la ville. Dans ce contexte, les acteurs humanitaires ont progressivement repris certains déplacements et activités dans les zones affectées par les restrictions de mouvement en vigueur depuis septembre dernier. Une reprise limitée de la circulation des populations civiles a également été observée sur les principaux axes concernés, tandis que le personnel des formations sanitaires périphériques a pu se rendre à Zémio pour s’approvisionner en médicaments. Aucun incident n’a été rapporté récemment sur ces itinéraires. Une organisation humanitaire a par ailleurs effectué des déplacements sur l’axe Zémio-Dembia afin de conduire des évaluations. Compte tenu de la volatilité persistante du contexte sécuritaire, les partenaires humanitaires continuent de suivre étroitement l’évolution de la situation et maintiennent les mesures de gestion des risques et de sécurité en vigueur.

BESOINS ET RÉPONSE HUMANITAIRE

Santé

Préfecture de la Haute-Kotto – Centre

Le 11 novembre 2026, le Fonds des Nations Unies pour la population (UNFPA) et son partenaire International Medical Corps (IMC) ont clôturé leur campagne de prise en charge holistique des femmes vivant avec une fistule obstétricale. Au total, 33 patientes ont bénéficié de soins spécialisés à Bria, avec un taux de réussite de 88 %. 15 autres patientes ont été confrontées à des difficultés de déplacement pour atteindre Bria depuis Ndele dans la préfecture du Bamingui-Bangoran. Afin d’améliorer l’accès à ces services dans cette préfecture, une seconde campagne de deux semaines a lieu à Ndele du 12 au 26 novembre 2026.

Multisectoriel

Préfecture de la Vakaga – Nord-Est

Le 11 novembre 2026, l’ONG COHEB, dans le cadre du projet de Travaux de haute intensité à main d’œuvre (THIMO) mis en œuvre à travers le Programme d’appui d’urgence à la stabilisation et au relèvement des réfugiés et des communautés hôtes dans le bassin du Lac Tchad (PASRRC), a procédé à une distribution monétaire au profit de 400 bénéficiaires, dont 150 réfugiés soudanais et 250 membres des communautés hôtes. A travers l’approche « travail contre rémunération », chaque bénéficiaire a reçu une assistance en espèces de 30 000 FCFA, visant à soutenir les moyens d’existence et à répondre aux besoins prioritaires des ménages vulnérables.

items.author: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations
items.content:
Countries: World, Angola, Benin, Botswana, Burkina Faso, Burundi, Cabo Verde, Cameroon, Central African Republic, Chad, Comoros, Congo, Côte d'Ivoire, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Djibouti, Equatorial Guinea, Eritrea, Eswatini, Ethiopia, Gabon, Gambia, Ghana, Guinea, Guinea-Bissau, Kenya, Lesotho, Liberia, Madagascar, Malawi, Mali, Mauritania, Mauritius, Mozambique, Namibia, Niger, Nigeria, Rwanda, Sao Tome and Principe, Senegal, Seychelles, Sierra Leone, Somalia, South Africa, South Sudan, Sudan, Togo, Uganda, United Republic of Tanzania, Zambia, Zimbabwe
Source: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations

Please refer to the attached file.

Synopsis (short abstract)

The cereal supply and demand balances included in this report present a subset of data from the FAO/GIEWS Country Cereal Balance System (CCBS) database created and continuously kept up to date by the Global Information and Early Warning System on Food and Agriculture (GIEWS) and Basic Foodstuffs teams of the Markets and Trade Division, with data since 1980. The report contains annual supply and utilization balances for the main cereals produced and consumed for over 220 countries/areas, from which (sub) regional and global aggregates are drawn.

This statistical report contains a subset of cereal country balance sheets (CCBS) data and presents updated cereal supply and demand balances for all sub-Saharan African countries. It complements the information of the FAO/GIEWS Crop Prospects and Food Situation report and is published four times a year with the same schedule.

This report is based on information available as at October 2026.

items.creator: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations
items.title: World: Food Price Monitoring and Analysis (FPMA) Bulletin #9, 12 November 2026
items.author: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations
items.content:
Country: World
Source: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations

Please refer to the attached file.

Synopsis (short abstract)

Global wheat and maize export prices declined in October 2026. Wheat prices fell amid subdued import demand and improving global production prospects, while maize prices declined from their September three‑year high amid seasonal harvest pressure in the United States of America and expectations of ample supplies from South America. Expectations of easing constraints on Black Sea export flows also weighed on wheat prices, although continued logistical disruptions in the region partly offset the downward pressure. By contrast, international rice prices increased, supported by harvest delays in some exporting countries, adverse weather conditions and rising production costs. In most domestic markets monitored by FAO, staple food prices remained relatively elevated in September and October 2026. In parts of East Africa and the Near East, conflict‑related market disruptions, currency depreciation and tight supplies continued to exert upward pressure on prices. In Far East Asia, weather-related production shortfalls and high production costs contributed to the increases in staple food prices, while in Eastern Europe, the Caucasus and Central Asia, high transport and import costs continued to exert upward pressure on domestic food prices. By contrast, the arrival of new harvests improved market supplies and contributed to seasonal price declines in parts of West Africa and Central and South America. However, strong demand, delayed harvests and unfavourable production prospects continued to drive price increases in some markets. In Southern Africa, ample domestic supplies and continued intra-regional trade helped contain seasonal price increases.

Synopsis (short abstract)
Global wheat and maize export prices declined in October 2026. Wheat prices fell amid subdued import demand and improving global production prospects, while maize prices declined from their September three‑year high amid seasonal harvest pressure in the United States of America and expectations of ample supplies from South America. Expectations of easing constraints on Black Sea export flows also weighed on wheat prices, although continued logistical disruptions in the region partly offset the downward pressure. By contrast, international rice prices increased, supported by harvest delays in some exporting countries, adverse weather conditions and rising production costs. In most domestic markets monitored by FAO, staple food prices remained relatively elevated in September and October 2026. In parts of East Africa and the Near East, conflict‑related market disruptions, currency depreciation and tight supplies continued to exert upward pressure on prices. In Far East Asia, weather-related production shortfalls and high production costs contributed to the increases in staple food prices, while in Eastern Europe, the Caucasus and Central Asia, high transport and import costs continued to exert upward pressure on domestic food prices. By contrast, the arrival of new harvests improved market supplies and contributed to seasonal price declines in parts of West Africa and Central and South America. In Southern Africa, ample domestic supplies and continued intra-regional trade helped contain seasonal price increases.

items.title: World: Crop Prospects and Food Situation Triannual Global Report No. 3, November 2026
items.author: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations
items.content:
Country: World
Source: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations

Please refer to the attached file.

Synopsis (short abstract)

The triannual Crop Prospects and Food Situation report provides a forward-looking global analysis of cereal production, market trends and acute food security conditions, with a particular attention on low-income food-deficit countries.

FAO estimates that 41 countries/territories require external assistance for food: 31 in Africa, eight in Asia, one in Latin America and the Caribbean, and one in Europe. Persisting conflicts and insecurity remain the primary drivers of the most severe levels of acute food insecurity, while weather shocks associated with the strong El Niño event are worsening conditions in several subregions. Looking ahead, El Niño-related impacts on production are expected to remain severe into 2027 in several subregions, likely aggravating acute food insecurity further.

The report also includes FAO's latest forecast for 2026 cereal production among the Low-Income Food-Deficit Countries (LIFDCs), pegged at 126.5 million tonnes, about 2 percent above both the 2025 level and the five-year average. The increase largely reflects a strong production recovery in Asia, particularly in Near East Asia, while production among African LIFDCs is expected to remain near-average.

items.creator: World Food Programme
items.title: World: WFP presenta su plan para 2027 para asistir a 91 millones de personas necesitadas ante la creciente amenaza de una crisis alimentaria mundial
items.author: World Food Programme
items.content:
Country: World
Source: World Food Programme

ROMA – El Programa Mundial de Alimentos de las Naciones Unidas (WFP) presentó hoy su Perspectiva Global para 2027, en el que detalla sus planes para asistir a 91 millones de personas necesitadas el próximo año, con un costo de poco más de USD 12.000 millones.

Sin embargo, el número de personas a las que WFP prevé brindar asistencia no refleja la magnitud total del hambre en el mundo. Según el Informe Global sobre las Crisis Alimentarias (GRFC), hasta 266 millones de personas enfrentaron hambre aguda en 2025, de las cuales se estima que 39 millones se encontraban en niveles de emergencia o peores.

En medio de este complejo contexto mundial y de las advertencias de que el mundo podría enfrentar su tercera gran crisis alimentaria mundial en seis años, WFP está reforzando su enfoque en medidas de eficiencia que le permitan ampliar su alcance y llegar a las personas más vulnerables. Esto incluye ampliar las iniciativas de acción anticipatoria, como la provisión de seguros y mecanismos de financiación previamente acordados que permitan a las comunidades prepararse mejor antes de que ocurran fenómenos climáticos extremos. WFP también aumentará el trabajo con socios locales y ampliará la asistencia basada en los mercados para aprovechar de manera más eficaz los recursos limitados.

“Para las personas más vulnerables del mundo, escapar del hambre aguda es cada vez más difícil”, afirmó Luke J. Lindberg, Director Ejecutivo de WFP. “Podemos proteger a las personas más vulnerables, pero para lograrlo se necesitarán un compromiso político sostenido, inversión y acción colectiva. Insto a otros a sumarse a nuestro llamado y actuar para garantizar que no haya más hambrunas, que los alimentos no vuelvan a utilizarse como arma y que cesen los ataques contra los trabajadores humanitarios”.

Casi el 72 por ciento de las necesidades de WFP para 2027 están destinadas a la respuesta a crisis, mientras que el 28 por ciento corresponde al fortalecimiento de la resiliencia. Cada contribución a WFP ayuda a salvar vidas hoy y, al mismo tiempo, crea las condiciones para que las comunidades sean más resilientes en el futuro.

# # #

El Panorama Global de WFP para 2027 puede consultarse aquí.

El Programa Mundial de Alimentos de las Naciones Unidas es la organización humanitaria más grande del mundo. Salva vidas en situaciones de emergencia y utiliza la asistencia alimentaria para construir un camino hacia la paz, la estabilidad y la prosperidad para las personas que se recuperan de conflictos, desastres y los efectos de fenómenos meteorológicos extremos.
